blocks.text: But Amos also reports two disasters brought on by the locust in his time. The first is in chapter four; it preceded the harvest and was joined with drought, mildew and blight. That locusts come forth more abundantly in drought we have already ^{b)} shown. And the wind קדים kadim drives them into Egypt, Exod. X, 13. From this same wind come שדפון, uredo [mildew], and ירקון, rubigo [blight]. Hence both evils are called ἀνεμοφθορία [anemophthoria] in Greek. In the Greek paraphrase this word occurs sometimes for ירקון, as in Agg. II, 18., and sometimes also for שדפון, as in Deut. XXVIII, 22. and 2 Par. VI, 28. Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion follow this in the very passage we are dealing with, that is, Amos IV, 8., where the Elders have ἐν πυρώσει [en pyrōsei]. And in Gen. XLI, 6. 27. the ears שדופות קדים, that is, struck with mildew by the wind kadim, are called in the Greek edition by a single word, ἀνεμόφθοροι [anemophthoroi]. By the same wind kadim, then, from which come drought, mildew and blight, the locusts too were brought into Judaea and consumed the gardens and vineyards, that is, the produce of the gardens and vineyards, and the figs and olives, that is, all the fruits of the trees. For the chief ones are named, and the rest are included under the name of gardens. Here gardens are paradises, as the Syriac translator rightly rendered it: that is, enclosed fields carefully [III, 322] planted with plants of every kind. Further, since the gazam here harmed neither pastures nor crops, but is said to have consumed only the fruits of the trees, it may have been peculiar to this species of locust that it fed on nothing other than the produce of trees. And the name itself suggests this. For, as noted in its place, among the Talmudists, Arabs and Ethiopians the verb גזם means to cut off and to lop, not just anything, but the branches of trees.
